concepts.name: GHI: Publishing Organizations and Mandate
key_dimensions: Co-published by Concern Worldwide (Ireland) and Welthungerhilfe (Germany) — NOT a UN body, a common UPSC trap
Annual release timeline (typically October) and its distinction from FAO's State of Food Security and Nutrition report
Non-governmental nature vs. indices published by World Bank, IMF, or UN agencies
Funding and methodology independence from national governments

concepts.name: GHI Score Calculation: The Four-Indicator Composite Formula
key_dimensions: Four indicators: Undernourishment, Child Stunting, Child Wasting, Child Mortality — and their individual weights (1/3, 1/6, 1/6, 1/3)
Why child mortality carries equal weight to undernourishment — the normative rationale
Score range: 0 (no hunger) to 100 (extreme hunger) — lower score is better, a frequent confusion point
Arithmetic vs. weighted aggregation and how it can mask sectoral improvements

concepts.name: Undernourishment Indicator: Definition and Data Source
key_dimensions: Defined as caloric intake below minimum dietary energy requirement for >1 year — FAO data source
Distinction from malnutrition (broader concept) and undernutrition (narrower)
Measured at population level using dietary surveys and food balance sheets — not individual clinical assessment
India's large population size disproportionately inflates global undernourishment figures — methodological critique

concepts.name: Child Wasting: Definition, Threshold, and GHI Weight
key_dimensions: Wasting = low weight-for-height in children under 5 — indicator of acute malnutrition
Carries 1/6 weight in GHI formula; threshold for 'extremely alarming' wasting >15%
Distinction from stunting (chronic) vs. wasting (acute) — UPSC frequently tests this confusion
India's wasting rate consistently among highest globally — implications for GHI rank

concepts.name: Child Stunting: Definition, Causes, and GHI Weight
key_dimensions: Stunting = low height-for-age in children under 5 — indicator of chronic malnutrition
Carries 1/6 weight in GHI formula; reflects long-term deprivation unlike wasting
Irreversibility of stunting after age 2 — the '1000-day window' policy implication
India's stunting decline trajectory vs. peer nations like Bangladesh and Nepal

concepts.name: Child Mortality Indicator in GHI: Rationale and Data Source
key_dimensions: Under-5 mortality rate used as proxy for inadequate nutrition AND broader environment of disease — dual signal
Data sourced from UN Inter-agency Group for Child Mortality Estimation (IGME)
Carries 1/3 weight — heaviest single component alongside undernourishment
Critique: mortality improvements may mask persistent malnutrition if disease control improves independently

concepts.name: GHI Severity Scale: Classification Categories and Cutoffs
key_dimensions: Five categories: Low (<10), Moderate (10–19.9), Serious (20–34.9), Alarming (35–49.9), Extremely Alarming (≥50)
India's persistent placement in 'Serious' category despite economic growth — decoupling debate
Countries with score <5 considered to have negligible hunger — typically high-income OECD nations
UPSC trap: 'Alarming' ≠ worst category; 'Extremely Alarming' is the highest severity

concepts.name: India's GHI Ranking: Trends, Controversies, and Government Response
key_dimensions: India ranked below neighbors Pakistan, Bangladesh, Nepal, Sri Lanka in recent editions — geopolitical sensitivity
Government of India's official rejection of methodology citing sample size of phone survey for undernourishment
Specific critiques: use of Gallup World Poll data (3,000 respondents) for a 1.4 billion population
Tension between GHI findings and government's NFSA/PDS claims of food security achievement

concepts.name: Methodological Critiques of GHI: Validity and Reliability Concerns
key_dimensions: Three of four indicators focus exclusively on children under 5 — does not capture adult hunger or women's nutrition
Undernourishment data lag (3-year average) may not reflect recent policy interventions
Binary framing: GHI measures hunger severity but not hunger causes (structural vs. transient)
Comparison challenge: countries with missing data are excluded, potentially skewing global rankings

concepts.name: GHI vs. FAO's State of Food Security and Nutrition in the World (SOFI) Report
key_dimensions: SOFI published by FAO, IFAD, UNICEF, WFP, WHO jointly — intergovernmental vs. GHI's NGO origin
SOFI focuses on SDG 2 monitoring; GHI is a composite index — different analytical purposes
Both use undernourishment data but SOFI provides disaggregated country-level food security analysis
UPSC trap: SOFI is not the same as GHI; different publishers, scope, and policy audience

concepts.name: GHI and SDG 2 (Zero Hunger): Linkages and Gaps
key_dimensions: SDG 2 targets: end hunger, achieve food security, improve nutrition, promote sustainable agriculture by 2030
GHI tracks progress toward SDG 2.1 (hunger) and 2.2 (malnutrition) but not 2.3–2.5 (agriculture targets)
GHI 2023 finding: at current pace, 58 countries will not achieve low hunger by 2030
Distinction between food security (access/availability) and nutritional security (quality/absorption)

concepts.name: Regional Patterns in GHI: Sub-Saharan Africa and South Asia
key_dimensions: Sub-Saharan Africa has highest average GHI scores globally — conflict, climate, governance nexus
South Asia paradox: economic growth coexisting with high child malnutrition — 'Asian enigma'
South Asia's child malnutrition rates higher than Sub-Saharan Africa despite higher GDP per capita — explained by sanitation, gender inequality, dietary diversity gaps
GHI as a tool to challenge the assumption that economic growth automatically reduces hunger

concepts.name: India's Nutrition Policy Architecture vs. GHI Indicators
key_dimensions: POSHAN Abhiyaan (National Nutrition Mission) targets: reduce stunting, wasting, anemia, low birth weight by 2–3% annually
ICDS (Integrated Child Development Services) and its role in addressing child wasting and stunting
National Food Security Act (NFSA) 2013 coverage — 75% rural, 50% urban — vs. persistent undernourishment
Mission Saksham Anganwadi and POSHAN 2.0 as convergence framework — whether GHI captures these interventions

concepts.name: Gender Dimensions of Hunger: Women's Nutrition and GHI Blind Spots
key_dimensions: GHI does not directly measure women's nutritional status despite women's nutrition being critical for child outcomes
Intergenerational malnutrition cycle: malnourished mothers → low birth weight infants → stunted children
NFHS data on anemia among women (>50%) — not reflected in GHI indicators
Policy implication: addressing only child indicators without women's nutrition is insufficient — GHI's structural limitation

concepts.name: Climate Change and Hunger: GHI's Environmental Framing
key_dimensions: GHI annual reports often carry thematic focus — e.g., 2022 report on conflict and climate as hunger drivers
Climate-induced food insecurity: droughts, floods affecting smallholder agriculture in GHI high-ranking countries
Distinction between chronic hunger (structural poverty) and acute hunger (climate/conflict shocks)
UPSC angle: how climate adaptation policies (PM-KUSUM, crop diversification) relate to hunger reduction

concepts.name: Conflict and Hunger Nexus in GHI Rankings
key_dimensions: Countries in active conflict (Yemen, Somalia, CAR, DRC) consistently rank in 'Alarming/Extremely Alarming' — GHI captures fragility
IPC (Integrated Food Security Phase Classification) used alongside GHI for conflict-affected nations — complementary tools
UPSC trap: GHI may understate hunger in conflict zones due to data unavailability — these countries sometimes excluded
R2P (Responsibility to Protect) and food as a weapon of war — international humanitarian law angle

concepts.name: Comparison of GHI with Global Food Security Index (GFSI)
key_dimensions: GFSI published by Economist Impact (formerly EIU) — private sector origin vs. GHI's NGO origin
GFSI measures four pillars: Affordability, Availability, Quality & Safety, Natural Resources & Resilience
GFSI ranks countries on food security capacity; GHI ranks on hunger outcomes — input vs. output distinction
India performs differently on GFSI vs. GHI — understanding why helps decode methodological differences

concepts.name: Historical Evolution of GHI: From 2006 to Present
key_dimensions: GHI first published in 2006 by IFPRI (International Food Policy Research Institute) — later transitioned to current publishers
2015 methodology revision: child mortality replaced as standalone indicator; wasting and stunting separated
Pre-2015 GHI not directly comparable to post-2015 GHI — a UPSC trap in trend analysis questions
Incorporation of SDG framework post-2015 into GHI's analytical structure

concepts.name: GHI Data Sources and the Role of NFHS in India's Assessment
key_dimensions: Child stunting and wasting data for India sourced from NFHS (National Family Health Survey) — conducted by IIPS
NFHS-5 (2019-21) data used in recent GHI editions — frequency of NFHS affects data currency
Government argument: NFHS data itself shows improvements, yet GHI rank worsened — methodology dispute
Role of DHS (Demographic and Health Surveys) program globally as standard data source for GHI child indicators

concepts.name: Zero Hunger Challenge and WFP's Role vs. GHI Framework
key_dimensions: UN Zero Hunger Challenge (2012) by Ban Ki-moon — five elements including zero stunted children under 2
WFP (World Food Programme) — Nobel Peace Prize 2020 — operational hunger relief vs. GHI's measurement role
UPSC trap: WFP does not publish GHI; it publishes its own hunger maps and food security assessments
Distinction between hunger measurement (GHI), hunger relief (WFP), and hunger policy (FAO/IFAD)
